what_it_measured.text: The primary efficacy endpoint was the percentage change in body weight,24 weeks post-intervention.

The unblinded coordinator functioned independently to ensure maintenance of investigator blinding throughout the study, thereby preserving the integrity of both subjective and objective outcome assessments.

dose.text: Participants initiated treatment at 0.25 mg/week for 1-4 weeks, 0.5 mg/week during 5-8 weeks, 1 mg/week during 9-12 weeks, 1.7 mg/week during 13-16 weeks, and 2.4 mg/week from week 17 through week 24.

route.text: Subcutaneous injections were administered once every week, either in the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm.

endpoint.text: The primary efficacy endpoint was the percentage change in body weight,24 weeks post-intervention.

Secondary endpoints included (i) the percentage of participants achieving >10% and >15% weight reduction, (ii) changes in BMI, waist circumference, and HbA1c, (iii) the rate of adverse events, and (iv) the percentage of participants developing anti-drug antibodies (ADAs).
Endpoints and assessments The primary endpoint of the trial was to assess the percentage body weight loss.

reported_results.text: Mean body mass index decreased by -4.93 ± 1.43 kg/m² in the test arm and -5.00 ± 1.50 kg/m² in the reference arm (p = 0.7128).
The least squaremean difference was 0.15% (-0.93 to 1.24), meeting the predefined non-inferiority criterion.
Mean percentage weight loss after 24 weeks was -14.39 ± 4.17% in the test arm and -14.61 ± 4.36% in the reference arm.
Results: Of the 249 randomized participants, 246 (98.8%) completed the study.
Synthetic semaglutide was established to be non-inferior if the lower bound of the one-sided 97.5% confidence interval for the between-group difference did not exceed 4.5%.
Between-group comparison showed comparable weight reduction (# p = 0.7790).

Mean percentage weight loss after 24 weeks was -14.39 ± 4.17% in the test arm and -14.61 ± 4.36% in the reference arm.
Results: Of the 249 randomized participants, 246 (98.8%) completed the study.
